theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before a machine is shut down for repair, what should you find out first?
options: The name of the company that first built the machine
Every energy source that feeds or is stored in it
How much the machine cost to buy when it was new
Which trainee used the machine last week

questions.stem: Where would you find the correct shutdown and isolation steps for a particular machine?
options: On the sales leaflet that came with the machine
From whoever is standing nearest to the machine
On the delivery note from the supplier's truck
In the isolation procedure and maker's manual

questions.stem: Who must be told before a machine is shut down for work?
options: The supervisor and the operators who use it
Only the store clerk who gives out the tools
Nobody, as long as the work is done quickly
Only the cleaner who works in that area

questions.stem: A machine has a main power supply and a separate control supply from another panel. What must you do?
options: Isolate the main supply only, as it is the biggest
Isolate the control supply only, as it starts the motor
Isolate and lock off both of the supplies
Isolate neither, and just press the stop button

questions.stem: Which of these could still feed power to a machine after its main supply is switched off?
options: A backup battery or a standby generator
The machine's nameplate and its warning labels
The light from the workshop windows
The paint on the machine's guards

questions.stem: What should each worker collect before an isolation?
options: A spare fuse, a roll of tape and a small torch
A neon screwdriver and a pair of pliers
A notebook, a pen and a phone charger
Their own lock, a tag and an approved tester

questions.stem: What is the correct way to stop a machine before isolating it?
options: Pull out its plug or cable while it is running
Open the isolator while it runs at full load
Use its normal stop, as the procedure says
Throw a cloth into the drive to slow it down

questions.stem: Why should a machine be stopped with its normal stop control before the isolator is opened?
options: So that the stop button gets regular use
So the isolator is not opened under load
So that the lights on the machine stay on
So that the isolator handle stays cool

questions.stem: An emergency stop button has been pressed and the machine has stopped. Is it safe to put your hands into the machine?
options: Yes, because an emergency stop always cuts off all power
Yes, as long as the red button stays pressed in
Yes, if the machine has been stopped for a minute
No, an emergency stop does not isolate the machine

questions.stem: A large, heavy part of a machine keeps turning after the machine is switched off. When can you start work on it?
options: Only when it has fully stopped by itself
Once it slows down, by holding it with a glove
At once, by jamming a bar in to stop it
When it is turning slowly enough to see

questions.stem: At which point should a machine be electrically isolated?
options: At the stop button on the control panel
At the machine's run/stop selector switch
At the isolator that cuts all live conductors
At the light switch for that part of the room

questions.stem: Why is a stop button on a control circuit NOT a safe point of isolation?
options: It is painted red, so it can be seen easily
It leaves the main supply on, so parts stay live
It is too far away from the machine to reach
It only works when the machine is running at full speed

questions.stem: When you lock off an isolator, what must you check?
options: That it is fully OFF and cannot be moved
That the handle has been cleaned and oiled
That the label on it is in the right colour
That the cover screws are all loosened

questions.stem: Why does each worker fit their own personal lock to the isolator, instead of sharing one lock?
options: So that the Centre can count how many locks it owns
So that the isolator is heavier and harder to move
So that each person can open it whenever they like
So it stays off until every worker has finished

questions.stem: Who may remove a personal lock from an isolator?
options: Any electrician on the same shift
Only the person who fitted it
The machine operator, when ready
The first person to finish work

questions.stem: What should be written on the tag fixed with your lock?
options: The machine's price and the date that it was bought
The weather today and the time your shift ends
Your name, the date, the reason and your contact
Only the words 'Do not touch', with no name

questions.stem: Why is a tag on its own, without a lock, not enough to keep an isolator off?
options: A tag is only a warning and cannot stop anyone
A tag can easily fall off when it rains in the yard
A tag costs much more to buy than a lock does
A tag must be renewed every hour of the job

questions.stem: Where a circuit is isolated by taking out its fuses, what else must be done?
options: Put the fuses back loosely so they are easy to find
Leave the fuses on top of the fuse board for others
Swap the fuses for bigger ones while they are out
Keep the fuses safe and lock or cap the holder

questions.stem: After locking off, why must you still prove the circuit dead?
options: To use up the tester's battery before it expires
To show the supervisor that you have your own tester
You may have the wrong isolator or another supply
To warm up the conductors before you touch them

questions.stem: Before and after proving dead, the voltage tester must be checked on:
options: a known live source of the right type
the circuit already proved dead
the metal frame of the machine
a fully charged phone battery

questions.stem: Your tester showed no voltage on the circuit, but when you checked it afterwards on the known live source, it did not work. What does this mean?
options: The circuit is dead, so the work can start
The test is not valid and must be done again
The live source is faulty, so the test was fine
The tester only needs a new battery later on

questions.stem: Which tester should be used to prove a circuit dead?
options: A neon test screwdriver with one probe
A continuity buzzer
A clamp meter on its current range
An approved two-pole voltage tester

questions.stem: When proving a single-phase supply dead, between which conductors should you test?
options: Line to neutral, then line to neutral again
Line to earth only, as earth is always dead
Line–neutral, line–earth and neutral–earth
Neutral to earth, then earth to the frame

questions.stem: After isolating and proving dead, what is the 'try' step?
options: Trying to open the isolator by force with a spanner
With all clear, pressing start: it must not run
Trying the tester on the earth bar to see if it works
Trying to remove another person's lock

questions.stem: Why can a motor speed drive (inverter drive) still be dangerous just after it has been isolated?
options: Its capacitors can hold a high voltage for some minutes
Its display screen stays lit for a while after switching off
Its cooling fan keeps turning for a few seconds
Its cover is made of metal and may feel warm

questions.stem: What is the safe way to deal with capacitors that may still be charged?
options: Short them out with a screwdriver blade
Touch them quickly with a gloved hand
Leave them alone, as capacitors cannot harm you
Wait, then test and discharge them properly

questions.stem: A machine has a heavy part held up by a spring. What must be done before working near it?
options: Oil the spring so that it moves more freely
Paint the spring red so that people see it
Release its tension or hold it with a block
Work fast so the spring has no time to move

questions.stem: Why must the air in a pneumatic line be released before a hose or fitting is taken off?
options: So that the air can be used again for the next job
Because the hose can whip and the air can injure you
So that the line does not rust inside while it is open
Because the compressor needs the air to cool itself

questions.stem: Why must you never feel for a hydraulic oil leak with your hand?
options: A fine jet of oil under pressure can pierce the skin
The oil will leave a stain on your work clothes for days
Your hand will be too greasy to hold your tools
The oil is too cold to feel with a bare hand

questions.stem: A press ram is raised. How should it be made safe before anyone reaches under it?
options: Ask someone to watch it while you work under it
Switch off the lights so nobody can start the press
Tie it up with a piece of rope from the store
Lower it, or hold it with a proper safety block

questions.stem: Why must an air compressor be isolated electrically before its receiver is drained?
options: Draining makes the motor run in the wrong direction
It may start by itself when the pressure falls
The drain valve only works with the power off
Water in the receiver can carry the electric current

questions.stem: A heating platen on a machine has just been running. What must you do before touching it?
options: Pour cold water on it to cool it quickly
Touch it quickly with a wet finger to test it
Let it cool and check its temperature
Wear cotton gloves and carry on at once

questions.stem: A pipe to a machine carries hot water or chemicals. How should it be isolated?
options: Close and lock its valves, then drain the line
Bend the pipe flat with a hammer to stop the flow
Wrap the pipe in tape where the work will be done
Open the valves fully so the line empties into the room

questions.stem: You are not sure that all the stored energy in a machine has been released. What should you do?
options: Start work, as most of it is probably gone
Touch the parts quickly to see if anything moves
Leave it for the next shift to find out
Stop and ask your supervisor before going on

questions.stem: Before removing your lock at the end of the job, what must you check first?
options: That the machine has been painted where you worked
That the next job has been written in the diary
That tools are removed and the guards are refitted
That your tester battery has been fully charged

questions.stem: Before the machine is switched back on, what must you make sure of?
options: That the lights in the area have been turned off
That everyone is clear and has been told
That the tags have been left on for the next job
That the guards are kept off for a test run

questions.stem: In which order is a machine usually returned to service?
options: Switch on first, refit the guards, then remove the locks
Check, refit guards, remove locks, restore, then test
Remove the locks, switch on, then pick up the tools
Test run with the guards off, then refit them later

questions.stem: You find a lock and tag on an isolator, but the person who fitted them has gone home. What should you do?
options: Tell the supervisor and follow the procedure
Cut the lock off with bolt cutters and then carry on
Remove the tag, but leave the lock where it is
Switch on, as the person must have finished

questions.stem: Why is a test run done after the work is finished?
options: To use up the old oil before the next service is due
To warm the machine up for the night shift
To see how fast the operator can work it
To check it works safely before handing it back

questions.stem: When handing a machine back, what should you tell the operator or supervisor?
options: Only the time of day that you finished the work
Nothing, as the machine is now working
What was done, and anything still to be fixed
The names of the tools you used on the job

questions.stem: Why is each isolation written in the isolation log?
options: So everyone knows what is isolated, by whom and why
So the Centre can charge the client for the locks
So the trainees get practice at their handwriting skills
So the machine's warranty is made longer

questions.stem: While a machine is shut down, you notice a damaged cable on it. What should you do?
options: Wrap tape round it quickly and say nothing about it
Report it and record it so that it is repaired
Leave it, as it is not part of your job today
Cut it out and leave the ends loose for later

questions.stem: What should be recorded when a machine is returned to service?
options: The colour of the locks that were used
The weather and the outside temperature that day
The names of everyone who walked past
The time, who restored it and the test result

questions.stem: Who should isolate a machine for maintenance?
options: Any person who happens to be standing nearby
The newest trainee, to give them practice
A trained person who is authorised to do it
Whoever arrives at the workshop first

questions.stem: While you are working on an isolated machine, someone asks you to check a part quickly with the power on. What should you do?
options: Do it quickly while someone watches the switch
Do it, as long as you stand on a dry rubber mat
Do it, but only use one hand to touch the part
Say you never work live, and ask for a safe way

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters LOTO stand for?
What is the name of the hinged steel clip, with several holes, that is fitted to an isolator's locking point so that more locks can be added?
What type of stored energy does a raised press ram or a lifted load have?
What written document gives permission to carry out high-risk work and lists the isolations that have been made?
What type of energy is held in a spinning flywheel or a moving conveyor?
What part of a hydraulic system can store oil under pressure even after the pump has stopped?
What kind of lock does each worker fit to an isolator during lock-off?
What kind of valve is opened to let trapped pressure out of a line after the line has been isolated?
What is the name of the solid plate fitted between pipe flanges to stop all flow in a line?
In a group isolation, the keys of all the isolation locks are put into one box, and every worker fits a lock to that box. What is this box called?
What do the letters PPE stand for?
What type of stored energy is held in a hot pipe or a hot heating platen?
What safety device on an air receiver opens by itself if the pressure gets too high?
When every energy source on a machine has been isolated and released, the machine is said to be in a 'zero ____ state'. What is the missing word?
What do the letters VFD stand for?

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would safely isolate an electrically driven machine before working on it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the machine's isolation procedure and drawings to find every energy source, and I tell the supervisor and the operators. I collect my own lock, tag and an approved two-pole voltage tester. I stop the machine with its normal stop control and wait until all moving parts have stopped. Then I switch off at the correct isolator, which cuts all the live conductors, and check that it is fully in the OFF position. I fit my personal lock and my tag, with my name, the date and the reason, so that nobody can switch it on. Next I check my voltage tester on a known live source to prove it works. I test at the machine between all the conductors, line to line, line to neutral and each line to earth, and find no voltage. Then I check the tester again on the known live source. With everyone clear, I press start to make sure the machine will not run, and return the controls to off. I deal with any stored energy before starting work.
markingPoints: Plans: finds every energy source, tells the supervisor and operators, collects lock, tag and approved tester
Stops the machine with its normal stop and waits until it is at rest
Switches off at the correct isolator, checks it is fully OFF, fits own lock and completed tag
Proves dead between all conductors with a tester checked on a known live source before and after
Does the try step with everyone clear, returns controls to off, and deals with stored energy

essays.stem: Explain the kinds of stored energy that can remain in a machine after it is isolated, and how each one is made safe.
essays.modelAnswer: Isolating the supply does not remove all the danger, because energy can be stored in the machine. Electrical energy can stay in capacitors, such as those in a motor speed drive. I wait the time stated by the maker, then test with an approved tester and discharge them with the proper tool if needed. Springs can be under tension or compression, so I release them as the manual says or hold them with a mechanical block. Compressed air and hydraulic oil can be trapped in pipes, cylinders and vessels, so I close and lock the valves, release the pressure and check that the gauges read zero. Raised parts, such as a press ram or a lifted load, can fall under their own weight, so I lower them to rest or hold them with proper safety blocks or pins. Flywheels and other heavy parts can keep turning, so I wait until they stop by themselves. Hot parts are left to cool. I check that each one is safe before I start work.
markingPoints: Capacitors: wait the stated time, test, and discharge properly
Springs: release the tension or hold with a mechanical block
Air and hydraulic pressure: close and lock valves, release the pressure, check gauges read zero
Raised parts (gravity): lower to rest or hold with proper blocks or pins
Moving and hot parts: wait until stopped and cooled; check each source before work

essays.stem: Describe how isolation is managed when several workers from different trades work on the same machine at the same time.
essays.modelAnswer: When several people work on one machine, each of them must be protected the whole time. The isolator is switched off and locked by the authorised person, and a multi-lock hasp is fitted to it, so that every worker can add their own personal padlock and tag. Each worker keeps the key to their own lock. The machine cannot be switched on until the last lock is removed, so nobody is put in danger when someone else finishes early. If the machine has many isolation points, a group lockbox is used: the isolation locks are fitted at each point, their keys go into the box, and each worker puts their own lock on the box. The isolations are listed in the isolation log or on the permit to work, and each worker signs on and signs off. Before starting, each worker may ask to see the machine proved dead. When a worker finishes, they remove only their own lock. Nobody else removes a lock, except through the Centre's formal procedure with the supervisor.
markingPoints: Isolator locked off with a hasp so each worker fits their own lock and tag
Each keeps their own key; the machine stays off until the last lock is removed
A group lockbox is used when there are many isolation points
Isolations recorded in the log or permit; workers sign on and off; may see it proved dead
Each removes only their own lock; any other removal only by formal procedure with the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain how you prove that a circuit is dead, and why the voltage tester is checked before and after the test.
essays.modelAnswer: Proving dead shows that the circuit really is dead after it has been isolated. The wrong isolator may have been switched off, there may be a second supply, or a switch may have failed, so I never trust the isolator alone. I use an approved two-pole voltage tester with fused leads and finger guards, not a neon screwdriver or a meter on the wrong range. First I check the tester on a known live source, or a proving unit, to show that it is working. Then I test at the point of work between every pair of conductors: on single-phase, line to neutral, line to earth and neutral to earth; on three-phase, each line to every other line, and each line to neutral and to earth. The tester must show no voltage each time. Then I check the tester again on the known live source. This shows that the tester did not fail during the test. If it did fail, the 'dead' result means nothing, and the test is done again with a good tester.
markingPoints: Why: the wrong isolator, a second supply or a failed switch could leave it live
Uses an approved two-pole voltage tester, not a neon screwdriver
Checks the tester on a known live source or proving unit before testing
Tests between every pair of conductors at the point of work
Checks the tester again afterwards, because a tester that failed makes the result worthless; retests if so

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan the shutdown of a machine for maintenance.
essays.modelAnswer: I find out what work is to be done and how long it will take. I read the machine's isolation procedure, the maker's manual and the drawings to find every energy source: the main electrical supply, any control or backup supply, compressed air, hydraulics, steam or water, and stored energy such as springs, raised parts and capacitors. I find each isolation point and check that it can be locked. I agree a time with the supervisor and tell the operators, so that production can be stopped in an orderly way and products are not spoiled. I check whether a permit to work is needed. I collect the right equipment: personal locks and tags, a hasp or lockbox, an approved voltage tester, blocks for raised parts and the PPE needed. I plan the order of shutdown and isolation, and I put up barriers and signs around the work area. I also plan how the machine will be restored and tested afterwards.
markingPoints: Finds out the work to be done and reads the procedure, manual and drawings
Lists every energy source, including stored energy, and each lockable isolation point
Agrees the time with the supervisor and tells the operators, so the stop is orderly
Checks for a permit and collects locks, tags, tester, blocks and PPE
Plans the order of shutdown, barriers and signs, and how the machine will be restored

essays.stem: Explain how a machine is safely returned to service after maintenance.
essays.modelAnswer: When the work is finished, I check that all tools, parts, rags and materials have been removed from the machine, and that the guards and covers are refitted and secure. I check that the area is clean and clear. I make sure everyone working on the machine has finished, and each person removes only their own lock and tag; the machine stays off until the last lock is removed. I tell the operators and everyone nearby that the machine is about to be started, and make sure they stand clear. Any blocks, props or blanks are removed, and energy is restored in the order given in the procedure. A competent person then runs the machine and checks that it works correctly and safely, including the stop button and the emergency stop. I record the work done, the test result and the time it was handed back in the log, and tell the supervisor about anything that still needs attention.
markingPoints: Tools and materials removed, guards and covers refitted, area clean and clear
Each person removes only their own lock; the machine stays off until the last lock is off
Operators and people nearby told and kept clear
Blocks and blanks removed; energy restored in the order the procedure gives
Test run by a competent person, including the stops; work recorded and handed back

essays.stem: Describe how you would safely isolate a compressed-air (pneumatic) system and the air compressor that feeds it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I tell the supervisor and the operators, because stopping the air will stop other machines too. An air compressor can start by itself when the pressure falls, so I isolate it electrically first: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after. Then I close the main air valve between the receiver and the line, and lock it closed with my lock and tag. I open the bleed valve on the part of the line I will work on and let the trapped air out slowly, keeping my face away. I check that the gauge reads zero and that cylinders have moved to rest or are blocked, because a cylinder can move when the air is let out. If I must work on the receiver itself, I release all its air through the drain or bleed valve and check that its gauge reads zero. I never point air at anyone, and I wear safety glasses and hearing protection.
markingPoints: Tells the supervisor and operators first
Isolates the compressor electrically first (it can start by itself), with full safe isolation
Closes, locks and tags the air valve
Releases the trapped air slowly and checks the gauge reads zero
Cylinders at rest or blocked, receiver drained if needed, PPE worn, air never pointed at anyone

essays.stem: Describe how to isolate a machine whose motor is fed from a motor speed drive (inverter drive), including how to deal with the stored charge in the drive.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the maker's manual and the warning label on the drive, which states how long to wait after switching off. I stop the motor with the normal stop control, so the drive slows it down. Then I switch off and lock off the isolator that feeds the drive, and fit my tag. I also isolate any separate control supply or other supply to the drive. The capacitors inside the drive can hold a dangerous voltage for several minutes, so I wait at least the time stated by the maker before opening the cover. Then I check my approved voltage tester on a known live source, test at the drive's input terminals and at the DC terminals the maker shows, to confirm there is no voltage, and then check the tester again. If any voltage remains, I wait longer or discharge it as the maker says, using the proper tool, never a screwdriver. I also make sure the motor cannot be turned by its load, because a turning motor can feed voltage back into the drive.
markingPoints: Reads the manual and the drive's label for the waiting time
Stops the motor normally, then isolates, locks and tags the drive supply and any other supply
Waits at least the stated time before opening the cover
Proves dead at the input and DC terminals with a tester checked before and after
Discharges properly if needed (never with a screwdriver) and stops the motor being turned by its load

essays.stem: Explain what you should do if the isolation cannot be done exactly as the procedure says, for example the isolator will not lock, your tester fails, or you find a supply that is not on the drawings.
essays.modelAnswer: If any step of the isolation cannot be done properly, I stop and do not start the work. I never carry on hoping it will be all right, and I never work live. If the isolator will not lock in the OFF position, or the lock does not fit, I tell my supervisor, so that another lockable isolation point can be used or the isolator can be repaired before work starts. If my tester fails, or does not work when I check it again after testing, the result cannot be trusted. I get another approved tester, check it on a known live source, and test again. If I find a supply that is not on the drawings or in the procedure, such as a cable from another panel or a backup supply, I treat the machine as live, report it, and wait until that supply has been found, isolated and locked too. The drawings and the procedure must then be corrected, and I write down what happened in the log.
markingPoints: Stops, does not start work, and never works live
Isolator will not lock: reports it; another lockable point is used or it is repaired first
Tester fails: gets another approved tester, checks it and tests again
Unknown supply: treats the machine as live, reports it, waits until it is isolated and locked
Drawings and procedure corrected and the event recorded

essays.stem: Describe the PPE and other safety precautions needed when shutting down and isolating machines, and explain why each is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: I wear safety glasses because springs, compressed air, hydraulic oil and broken parts can fly out. Safety boots protect my feet from dropped tools and heavy parts. Gloves suited to the job protect my hands from sharp edges, hot parts and oil, but I do not wear loose gloves near any part that could still move. Hearing protection is needed near compressors and noisy plant. Where the procedure asks for it, I wear the electrical PPE it lists for testing. I tie back long hair and remove jewellery and loose clothing so nothing can be caught. As well as PPE, I put up barriers and warning signs around the work area to keep others away, and I keep the area clean and dry so that nobody slips. I use only approved locks, tags and testers in good condition. I make sure there is good lighting. I know where the first-aid kit, the fire extinguisher and the exits are, and I do not work alone on a dangerous isolation.
markingPoints: Safety glasses against flying parts, air and oil
Safety boots, suitable gloves (not loose near moving parts) and hearing protection, with reasons
Hair tied back; no jewellery or loose clothing
Barriers and signs, good housekeeping and lighting
Approved locks, tags and testers; first aid and extinguisher known; not working alone

practical1.title: Shut down, isolate, lock off and prove dead a motor-driven machine, then return it to service
practical1.brief: The assessor chooses a motor-driven machine at the Centre (for example a bench drill, a pedestal grinder, or a motor on the training bench fed through a starter and a lockable isolator), with its isolation procedure. As a group: (1) fill in an isolation sheet listing every energy source and isolation point, and tell the 'operator' (the assessor) that the machine will be shut down; (2) stop the machine with its normal stop control and wait for it to come to rest; (3) switch off at the isolator, fit a multi-lock hasp, and each member fits their own lock and completed tag; (4) one member at a time, while the assessor watches, checks the voltage tester on a proving unit or known live source, proves dead at the machine's terminals, and checks the tester again; (5) with everyone clear, try the start button to show that the machine will not start, and return the controls to off; (6) carry out a simple task the assessor sets, such as removing and refitting a guard cover; (7) return the machine to service: tools out, guards on, area clear, each member removes only their own lock, the instructor restores the supply, and the group watches the test run. Fill in the isolation log. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A motor-driven machine with a lockable isolator, chosen and checked by the instructor
The machine's isolation procedure and a blank isolation sheet
A multi-lock hasp, and a personal padlock and tag for each member
An approved two-pole voltage tester and a proving unit
Hand tools for the set task, barrier tape and warning signs
Safety glasses, safety boots and any other PPE the procedure asks for
photos: The completed isolation sheet listing each energy source and isolation point
The machine stopped, with barriers and signs round the work area
The isolator in the OFF position with the hasp, every member's lock and their tags
A member checking the tester on the proving unit before the test
A member proving dead at the machine's terminals
The try step: start pressed with everyone clear, and the machine not running
Guards refitted and tools removed before the locks come off
The completed isolation log after the test run
checklist: Listed every energy source and isolation point correctly on the isolation sheet
Told the operator, and stopped the machine with its normal stop, waiting until it came to rest
Switched off at the correct isolator and checked that it was fully OFF
Fitted their own lock and a completed tag (name, date, reason, contact)
Checked the tester on a known live source or proving unit before and after proving dead
Proved dead between every pair of conductors at the point of work
Carried out the try step safely and returned the controls to off
Before restoring: removed tools, refitted guards, cleared the area and removed only their own lock
Filled in the isolation log correctly
safety: Never work live: no work starts until the machine is locked off and proved dead
Only the instructor restores the supply; nobody removes another person's lock
Keep hands, hair and loose clothing away from the machine until it has fully stopped
Use only an approved two-pole voltage tester with finger guards, never a neon screwdriver
Keep the barriers and signs in place until the machine has been handed back
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Isolate a machine with stored energy: air pressure, a raised part and a speed drive
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a machine or training rig with more than one energy source, for example the Centre's air compressor feeding a pneumatic cylinder rig, a part that can be raised, and a motor fed by a speed drive. As a group: (1) make an energy map, a simple drawing or list of the machine showing every energy source (electrical supply, control supply, compressed air, the raised part, any springs, the capacitors in the drive, any hot parts) and how each will be isolated or released; (2) isolate the electrical supplies to the compressor and the drive, lock and tag them, and prove dead as the Centre's procedure says (the compressor must be isolated before any air is released, because it can start by itself); (3) close and lock the air valve and release the trapped air until the gauge reads zero; (4) lower the raised part to rest or fit the safety block; (5) wait the time stated on the drive's label and then, while the instructor watches, test that the drive's stored charge has gone; (6) check every item on the energy map and sign it; (7) restore everything in the right order with the instructor. Each member is responsible for at least one energy source and explains it to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A machine or rig with several energy sources (for example an air compressor and cylinder rig, a raised part and a motor speed drive), set up by the instructor
The maker's manuals and the Centre's isolation procedure
Personal padlocks, tags and a multi-lock hasp; lockable valve covers if needed
An approved two-pole voltage tester and a proving unit
A safety block or prop suited to the raised part
Blank energy map and the isolation log
Safety glasses, hearing protection, safety boots and gloves
photos: The finished energy map, showing every energy source and how it is controlled
The compressor and drive isolators locked and tagged
The air valve closed, locked and tagged
The air gauge reading zero after the trapped air was released
The raised part lowered to rest or held by the safety block
The drive's warning label, and the test showing no stored charge
The energy map with every item checked and signed
The machine restored and running, with the area clear
checklist: Found every energy source, including stored energy, and drew a correct energy map
Isolated the compressor electrically before any air was released, and explained why
Locked and tagged each isolation point with their own lock and tag
Proved dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after
Released the trapped air safely, face away from the outlet, and checked the gauge read zero
Lowered or blocked the raised part correctly
Waited the time on the drive's label before testing for stored charge
Explained their own energy source and how it is controlled clearly to the assessor
Restored the energy sources in the right order with the instructor, after checking the area was clear
safety: Never work live, and never assume a machine is dead because it is quiet
The air compressor can start by itself: isolate it before any air is released
Never point compressed air at anyone; wear safety glasses and hearing protection
Never put any part of your body under a raised part unless it is lowered or properly blocked
Never short out capacitors with a screwdriver; wait the stated time and test
Only the instructor restores the supplies; each member removes only their own lock
